en: Warm ocean water evaporates into vapor, rises, and cools to condense into liquid droplets that form clouds.
Magma cooling and solidifying beneath the Earth's surface forms coarse-grained intrusive igneous rocks like granite.
Plant roots grow into rock cracks and pry them apart, physically weathering the stone into soil particles.
The Sun's immense gravity pulls planets inward while their forward velocity keeps them moving in elliptical orbits.
The Moon's orbit around Earth changes the sunlit portion visible from our planet, creating the lunar phases.
The Sun heats Earth's surface unevenly, causing warm air to rise and cooler air to rush in as wind.
Tectonic plates sticking together build up stress until the rock fractures, releasing energy as seismic earthquake waves.
A massive star exhausts its nuclear fuel, causing its core to collapse and explode outward as a supernova.
The Gulf Stream carries warm equatorial water northward, transferring heat that warms the climate of Western Europe.
Intense subterranean heat and pressure bake and squeeze existing rocks, recrystallizing them into metamorphic rocks like marble.
Rainwater seeps through porous soil and percolates downward, filling underground aquifers that store liquid freshwater for later use.
Warm ocean water evaporates into vapor, and the vapor condensing into clouds releases heat that fuels typhoon winds.
